title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 3 + Sol.: OT elects and meritorious cause
pass_a_gloss:
Obj. 3. If in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting that sacrifice, there is a certain special intention concerning vivifying and infallibly saving all the elect by the virtue and merit of the same sacrifice, we seem to exclude from this special privilege the elect under the Old Testament, who were born and died before this sacrifice of Christ exhibited on the cross.

Sol. As to the account of general sufficiency or of special efficacy, I answer that Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the external act of exhibition, which it had and has under the New, after Christ was really exhibited and offered on the cross. Just as therefore to the elect under the N.T. special grace is derived from the special intention of God from the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so to the elect under the O.T. special grace flowed from the special will of the same God from the merit of the same sacrifice afterward to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the origin of the world, both in the preparation of his will and in the acceptance of the Father's will. And so it is to be observed here that there is one account of that cause which operates Physically or naturally, another of that which operates meritoriously or morally. A cause acting physically must be actually posited before some effect is produced by its virtue: but a cause acting meritoriously or morally, such as Christ's passion, can produce an effect before it actually exists, if it at least precedes in the cognition and acceptance of him to whom it pertains to dispense the benefits of his grace to human beings with regard to the same. For in this matter a Meritorious cause has a certain kinship with a Final cause, which, not yet actually existing, but only foreseen and foreconsidered, validly moves the agent to doing this or that. In this way we say that Christ's passion, and the merits depending on the same, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob and not to Esau, had the account of a moving cause of God to gifting Jacob that special grace which he denied to Esau. Rightly Suarez, in 3, question 49, article 4, in the commentary: That special love by which, on account of Christ's merits, whether exhibited or foreseen, God sanctifies human beings and reconciles them to himself, can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or the love (or election) of God freely terminated toward us.
pass_b_english:
Obj. 3. If Christ in offering himself, and God in accepting that sacrifice, had a special intention to vivify and surely save all the elect by that sacrifice's virtue and merit, we seem to shut Old Testament elect out of the privilege — those born and dead before Christ's sacrifice was shown on the cross.

Sol. On general sufficiency or special efficacy I answer: Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the outward act of exhibition, that it has under the New after Christ was really shown and offered on the cross. Just as special grace reaches New Testament elect from God's special intention by the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so special grace flowed to Old Testament elect from the same God's special will by the merit of that same sacrifice still to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the world's beginning, both in the readiness of his will and in the Father's acceptance. Note the difference: a cause that works physically or naturally must already be in act before its power yields an effect; a cause that works meritoriously or morally — such as Christ's passion — can yield an effect before it actually exists, if it at least stands beforehand in the knowledge and acceptance of him who, with regard to it, dispenses the benefits of his grace. Here a meritorious cause is kin to a final cause: not yet existing in act, but only foreseen and weighed, it still moves the agent to act. So we say Christ's passion and its dependent merits, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob, not Esau, moved God to give Jacob the special grace he denied Esau. Suarez puts it well (In 3, q. 49, art. 4, comm.): that special love by which, for Christ's merits — exhibited or foreseen — God sanctifies and reconciles people can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or God's love (or election) freely fixed on us.
source_text:
Obj. 3. Si in Christo seipsum offerente, Deoque illud sacrificium acceptante, sit specialis quaedam intentio de vivificandis & infallibiliter salvandis electis omnibus virtute & merito ejusdem sacrificii, videmur ab hoc speciali privilegio excludere electos sub Veteri Testamento, qui nati ac denati fuerunt ante hoc sacrificium Christi in cruce exhibitum.

Sol. Quoad rationem sufficientiae generalis sive efficaciae specialis, respondeo, Christi sacrificium eandem virtutem habuisse sub Veteri Testamento, ante externum actum exhibitionis, quam habuit & habet sub Novo, post Christum realiter in cruce exhibitum & oblatum. Sicuti igitur ad electos sub N. T. ex speciali intentione Dei derivatur gratia specialis a merito hujus sacrificii jam actu exhibiti, ita ad electos sub V. T. ex speciali ejusdem Dei voluntate dimanavit gratia specialis a merito ejusdem sacrificii postmodum exhibendi. Christus enim erat Agnus occisus ab origine mundi, tam in praeparatione voluntatis suae, quam in acceptatione voluntatis Paternae. Est itaque hic observandum, aliam esse rationem causae ejus quae operatur Physice sive naturaliter, aliam ejus quae operatur meritorie sive moraliter. Causa physice agens, actu ponatur est necesse, priusquam ejus virtute effectum aliquod producatur: at causa agens meritorie sive moraliter, qualis est passio Christi, potest effectum producere priusquam actu exsistat, si praecedat saltem in ejus cognitione & acceptatione ad quem spectat ejusdem intuitu beneficia gratiae suae hominibus dispensare. Nam hac in re causa Meritoria habet cognationem quandam cum causa Finali, quae nondum actu exsistens, sed tantummodo praevisa & praeconsiderata, valide movet agentem ad hoc vel illud agendum. Hoc modo dicimus passionem Christi, meritaque ab eadem dependentia, praevisa ut Deo offerenda & applicanda specialiter Jacobo, & non Esavo, habuisse rationem causae moventis Deum ad donandum Jacobo illam specialem gratiam, quam Esavo negavit. Recte Suarez, in 3. qu. 49. art. 4. in comm. Illa specialis dilectio, qua propter merita Christi, sive exhibita sive praevisa, Deus homines sanctificat, & sibi reconciliat, potest cadere sub meritis Christi, sive promerendo nobis effectum illius dilectionis, sive dilectionem (vel electionem) Dei ad nos libere terminatam.
